title: The Reason Smart People Aren't As Articulate As They Think
author: Vicky Zhao
summary: Argues that the most costly communication failure is the one that does not look like a failure: everyone nods, agrees, and then delivers against different definitions of the same word. She calls this invisible drag, and opens on her own example — she asked her team for something 'quickly', meaning fast AND client-ready, and got fast. The fix is concept anchoring: before the conversation moves on, name the words that carry multiple meanings and define them for the room. Her simplest technique is the two-part split — say what you don't mean, then what you do. The problem worsens with seniority, because nobody asks a senior person what they meant by 'quickly'.
takeaways: Invisible drag is failure that presents as agreement. Nobody objects, everyone nods, and the divergence only surfaces when the work comes back wrong and the time is already spent.
Her worked example: she said 'quickly' meaning fast and client-ready; the team heard speed alone and delivered in an hour. Both parties were right about what was said.
Ordinary words carry incompatible readings. 'Priority' means drop everything to one person and move it up a list to another. 'Effort' means more hours to one and more thinking to another.
It gets worse with seniority: nobody asks a senior person what they meant, because the question sounds silly. 'They nod, they take the concept with them, and they figure it out on their own.'

The two-part split: when you use a key concept, split it in half — what you don't want, then what you do. 'By push, I don't mean stay here until 2:00 a.m... I mean push the quality that we can deliver within the time allowed.'
Trap one, TIME HORIZON. Always clarify now versus later, short versus long term. A decision about results today and a decision about ROI in a year lead to different work.

Trap two, LEVELS OF ANALYSIS. People naturally work at the level their experience sits — UX at customer level, strategy at system level, frontline at individual level. Naming which levels are in scope aligns them without correcting anyone.
She names 10 such traps and covers two, with the rest behind a download — worth knowing the framework is partial as presented.
The leadership reframe: 'why don't they think for themselves' is usually a missing-context problem, not a capability problem.
quotes: This is what I call the invisible drag. Probably one of the worst failures you can have in communication because it doesn't seem like a failure and yet the results push you back.
To me, you quickly is fast and client ready, right? But that's not what I said. I just said quickly.
This problem gets worse the more senior you become... it just sounds like such a silly idea. So what they do is they nod, they take the concept with them, and they figure it out on their own.
One half is about what you don't want and the other half is about what you do want.
As it is with using AI, our smart intern needs a bit of context. With real humans, you need to also share context.
The sharpest thinker and communicator are not the ones that speak a lot or the ones that speak too little... It's the one that's focused on clarifying and aligning everyone in the conversation.
bestIdeas: Define the ambiguous word for the room before the conversation moves on. Cheap, fast, and it converts a downstream rework into a five-second clarification — directly applicable to any meeting establishing new ways of working.
Say what you don't mean first. Negation narrows faster than definition, because it removes the reading the listener was about to take.

Naming levels of analysis aligns a mixed room without correcting anybody. Everyone contributes at the level they know; stating which levels are in scope makes those contributions connect rather than compete.
Treat 'they didn't think for themselves' as a context defect. It moves the fix from performance management to something the leader can actually do.
The same discipline you apply to prompting an AI applies to briefing a person. If you would give a model context, give a colleague the same.
tools: None named. The techniques are the artefact — the two-part split, time horizon, levels of analysis.
method: 1. Spot the load-bearing word. Before agreement is reached, identify which key concept in the conversation carries multiple plausible meanings.
2. Define it for the room: 'for our context, this is what I mean'.
3. Use the two-part split — state what you do NOT mean, then what you DO. 'By problem, I don't mean the surface problem with the symptoms. I mean the structural problem causing them.'
4. If you cannot see how to split it, apply trap one — TIME HORIZON. Now or later? Results today, or ROI in a year?
5. Or apply trap two — LEVELS OF ANALYSIS. Name which levels are in scope: individual, customer, system, market.
6. Do this before the conversation moves on, not after the work comes back.
